summary: Defines an email header field for recording the results of message authentication checks, so filters and mail programs can show or use them. This is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 6577, and it was replaced by RFC 7001.

plainLanguage.summary: When a mail server checks a message, it learns things: the sending domain's policy says this server may send for it, the signature checks out, the reverse DNS agrees. The Authentication-Results header is where the server writes those answers down, so that a program further along the chain can act on them.

questions: how do mail servers record spf and dkim results
what does dkim pass mean in email headers
subtitle: One mail header that says what each authentication check found.

tldr.problem: Mail servers can check whether a message really came from the domain it claims, but there was no common place to write down the answers, so each mechanism had its own header field and only carried its own result.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an Authentication-Results header field, a structured field naming the authenticating service and then listing method=result statements for each check, together with the properties that were evaluated.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5451 is a Proposed Standard from April 2009 and has been obsoleted by RFC 7001, which restates the header field. The unit metadata also lists RFC 6577 as updating it.

today: RFC 5451 is a Proposed Standard from April 2009, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 7001, which restates the Authentication-Results header field; the unit metadata also lists RFC 6577 as updating it. The RFC itself notes that the header field carries no integrity or validation mechanism of its own, so its presence must be trusted implicitly.

sections.title: Why a Common Header for Authentication Results
sections.content:
The RFC defines a header field for electronic mail messages that presents the results of a message authentication effort in a machine-readable form. The intent is to create a place to collect that data when authentication mechanisms are in use, so that a Mail User Agent and downstream filters can make filtering decisions or give the user a recommendation about the validity of the message's origin and possibly of the integrity of its content. End users are not expected to consume the header field directly; it is for programs that will then render the information in a human-usable form.

The header is expected to serve three purposes: conveying the results of various authentication checks applied by upstream filters and transfer agents to mail user agents and downstream filters within the same trust domain; providing a common location within a message for that data; and creating an extensible framework for reporting new authentication methods as they emerge.

The RFC stresses that the mere presence of the header field does not mean its data is valid, only that something upstream is asserting validity based on one or more schemes. For a consumer to treat the assertions as valid there must be an assessment of the trust relationship between the agents involved. It also says the memo does not discuss how the data should be used, since what filtering decisions are appropriate is a matter of local policy and user interface design.

The RFC distinguishes authorization from authentication. Authorization is the establishment of permission to use a resource or represent an identity, and in this context indicates that a message from a particular domain arrived by a route the domain explicitly approved. Authentication is the assertion of validity of a piece of data about a message, or of the message in its entirety. SPF and Sender-ID are authorization mechanisms: they express whether the sending domain authorized the connecting client to relay on its behalf, but validate no property of the message itself. DKIM is agnostic about routing but uses cryptographic signatures to authenticate the agents claiming responsibility for the message and to ensure it was not modified in transit. Because the signatures are not tied to SMTP connections, they can be added by the originating domain, by intermediate servers such as mailing lists, or by both. Rather than create a separate header field for each class of solution, the RFC groups them into one.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is a place to write down what the checks found, so later programs do not have to repeat them. It is not a guarantee on its own: only the server that wrote it knows whether to trust it.

sections.title: The Format of the Header Field
sections.content:
The field is called Authentication-Results and is a structured header field, so all the related definitions apply to it. It should be added at the top of the message as it transits the transfer agents that do authentication checks, so that some idea of how far away the checks were done can be inferred. It is therefore treated as a trace field.

The value consists of an authentication identifier, an optional version, and then a series of method=result statements saying which authentication methods were applied and what each returned. For each applied method there may also be an optional free-form reason string and optional property=value statements indicating which message properties were evaluated to reach the conclusion. The header field may appear more than once in a message, or more than one result may be represented in a single field, or a combination of the two.

The property statements have a type and a name. The type is one of smtp, meaning a parameter to an SMTP command, header, meaning a value taken from a message header field, body, meaning some property of the message body, or policy, meaning a policy decision not specific to any extractable property. A method that would normally report, say, header.From but finds no From field can use policy to say that no conclusion about authenticity could be reached. The type and property values are case-insensitive, and the property part may be omitted entirely when the method had a result to report but could extract no properties.
sections.plainLanguage: The header reads as a list of checks and their outcomes, and after each outcome it may list which parts of the message were looked at, such as a header field name or an SMTP command parameter.

sections.title: Result Values for Each Method
sections.content:
Every header field begins with an authentication identifier, the authserv-id, which gives a unique reference to the authenticating service within a given administrative management domain. The uniqueness must be guaranteed by the domain that generates it, and it is meant to be machine-readable rather than meaningful to users. Mail user agents and downstream filters should use it to decide whether to use the data. For simplicity and scalability it should be a common token used throughout the domain, such as the DNS domain name; for tracing it may instead be the hostname of the server that did the check. The RFC explains that a hierarchical identifier is easier for large sites, since related trusted systems can be grouped under one parent identifier, whereas a flat namespace needs each trusted system listed separately.

Each method returns one of a set of result values. DKIM and DomainKeys use none for a message that was not signed, pass for a signature that was acceptable and verified, fail for an acceptable signature that failed verification, policy for a signature that was not acceptable to the verifier, neutral for a signature that could not be processed, temperror for a failure that is likely transient such as a temporary inability to fetch a public key, and permerror for an unrecoverable failure such as a missing required header field. DKIM advises that a message failing verification should be treated as unsigned; reporting fail lets the receiver decide, while reporting neutral or none preempts that choice.

SPF and Sender-ID use none when no policy records were published, neutral when the sending domain says it cannot or will not assert, pass when the client is authorized, policy when the algorithm says pass but local policy disagrees, hardfail when the client is explicitly not authorized, softfail when the domain believes it was not authorized but is unwilling to assert strongly, plus temperror and permerror. The iprev method, which checks that the reverse and forward DNS lookups for the connecting address agree, has pass, fail, temperror and permerror, and no none, because every connection has an IP address. SMTP authentication uses none, pass, fail, temperror and permerror.
sections.plainLanguage: Each check reports one word. The important distinction is between a definite answer, a temporary failure that might be worth retrying, and a permanent one. The header also names the server that did the check, so a reader can decide whether to believe it.

sections.title: Adding the Header Field to a Message
sections.content:
The RFC makes no attempt to rank the authentication methods, so the order in which the methods and results appear must not be used to imply that one is stronger than another. The consumer must interpret each result on its own terms.

A compliant transfer agent must add the header field after performing one or more authentication tests, saying which agent performed the test, which test was applied and what the result was. If it applies more than one test it must add the field once per test or once with all the results, and it must not add a result to an existing header field. It may add the field with only the authentication identifier, to say explicitly that no authentication schemes were applied before delivery.

The field should be inserted at the top of the message, above any other trace fields the agent prepends, so that fields that can be trusted are easy to pick out. An agent must not include data it has not authenticated. For example, if a basic SPF result were relayed claiming an authenticated address specification, the local part of that address has in fact not been authenticated.

Consumer-side rules are just as strict. Mail user agents and downstream filters should not interpret the field unless specifically instructed to do so by the user or administrator, and not by default, because a hostile agent can forge the field and a non-conformant server will not strip it. They should not interpret it unless the authentication identifier it bears appears to be one used within their own domain as configured. They must ignore any result using a result code or property type that is not registered, and any result for a method they do not support. They should ignore instances found inside message/rfc822 attachments.
sections.plainLanguage: The server that adds the field writes it at the top of the message and only reports what it actually checked. The program that reads it should only trust it when the user or administrator has said which identifiers to trust.

sections.title: Removing the Header Field
sections.content:
For security reasons, a compliant transfer agent must delete any instance of the header field that claims to have been added within its own trust boundary but did not come from another trusted agent. An agent for example.com receiving a message must delete any instance bearing an identifier saying it was added within example.com, before adding its own. That may mean each agent needs a list of the internal agents known to be compliant.

For simplicity and maximum security a border agent may remove all instances of the field on mail crossing into its trust boundary. That conflicts with the wish to keep results from trusted external service providers, and it can invalidate signed messages whose signature covered the removed field. A more robust border agent could allow a specific list of authenticating agents whose information is let in and remove the rest. Removing a field that was covered by a DKIM signature may invalidate that signature, which can be desirable, since there is little value in validating a signature on a message with forged headers.

An agent should remove any instance of the field bearing a version it does not support, and must remove such a header if the SMTP connection relaying the message is not from a trusted internal agent.

The RFC's own security section lists the ways the field can be abused. A forged header field is the main one: a malicious user could forge a field using the DNS domain of the receiving domain as the authserv-id and claim the message was properly authenticated, and a non-conformant agent would fail to strip it, so the reader might wrongly trust it. That is why the handling of the field should not be enabled by default. The RFC lists several possible fixes, among them a digital signature protecting the header field, and it notes that if the internal agents are compliant and use their own host names or the domain's DNS domain as the identifier, the field should always appear above a Received header added by a trusted agent, which can be used as a test of validity.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the field carries no protection of its own, a server that receives mail from outside must delete any copy claiming to be from inside, or a stranger could write one and have it believed.

Authentication-Results: example.com;
          spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=example.net
Received: from dialup-1-2-3-4.example.net
              (dialup-1-2-3-4.example.net [192.0.2.200])
          by mail-router.example.com (8.11.6/8.11.6)
              with ESMTP id g1G0r1kA003489;
          Fri, Feb 15 2002 17:19:07 -0800
From: sender@example.net

items.label: Verified
items.desc: The message was signed, the signature was acceptable to the verifier, and it passed the verification tests.

items.label: Failed
items.desc: The message was signed and the signature was acceptable, but it failed the verification tests.

items.label: Not acceptable
items.desc: The message was signed but the signature was not acceptable to the verifier.

items.label: Could not be processed
items.desc: The signature contained syntax errors or could not otherwise be processed. Also used for other failures not covered elsewhere.

items.label: Temporary error
items.desc: The message could not be verified because of an error that is likely transient, such as a temporary inability to retrieve a public key. A later attempt may produce a final result.

items.label: Permanent error
items.desc: The message could not be verified because of an unrecoverable error, such as a required header field being absent.
